lesson.title: Banking Burstiness: Inside the Token Bucket Algorithm
lesson.summary: Token bucket shaping accumulates permission to send at a steady rate but banks unused permission up to a cap, letting a flow enforce a long-run average rate while still allowing short bursts when credit has built up.
lesson.body:
A token bucket works from a simple accounting rule. Tokens are generated at a fixed rate r and added to a bucket that can hold at most b tokens; once the bucket is full, newly generated tokens are simply discarded rather than overflowing anywhere. Sending one unit of data, commonly one packet or one byte depending on how the bucket is defined, requires spending one token. If the bucket currently holds enough tokens, the data is sent immediately and the tokens are removed. If it does not, the sender must wait for more tokens to accumulate, which is the shaping behavior, or in a policing context the excess is dropped or marked instead.

A concrete trace makes the behavior exact. Suppose the refill rate is r equals 2 tokens per second, the bucket capacity is b equals 4 tokens, and the bucket starts full. A burst of six packets, each needing one token, arrives all at once at time t equals 0. Packets 1 through 4 each find a token waiting and depart immediately, draining the bucket from 4 down to 0, all at t equals 0. Packet 5 has no token available and must wait for the next one to be generated, which happens at t equals 0.5 seconds at a refill rate of 2 per second, so packet 5 departs at t equals 0.5. Packet 6 waits for the following token and departs at t equals 1.0. The full departure sequence is 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1.0. Averaged over any sufficiently long window the sending rate converges to r, 2 packets per second, but the bucket's saved-up capacity let the first four packets leave as an instantaneous burst, completely free of the steady-rate limit that governed everything after it.

That burst allowance is not a flaw, it is the entire design intent. Real applications are naturally bursty, a TCP window opening up, a video encoder's keyframe, a page render flushing several resources at once, and forcing perfectly uniform spacing on all of that, which is what leaky bucket does in the next chapter, adds delay that is often unnecessary if the sender has been idle and has built up unused capacity. Token bucket's rule amounts to: if you were quiet for a while and accumulated credit, you may spend that credit in a burst, and only after the credit runs out are you throttled down to the sustained rate r.

The two parameters r and b are worth remembering by name, because they reappear later in this unit. They are literally the numbers that describe a traffic contract enforced by shaping, and they are also the shape of the flow specification that IntServ's RSVP signaling, covered further ahead, uses to describe how much of a reservation a flow is actually asking for.
